raw_case_text:
A 69-year-old female presented with a 1-month history of hoarseness and post-nasal drip. Her past history included a 10-year history of moderate persistent asthma which required a short course of oral prednisolone one to two times per year. In addition, she suffered from gastro-esophageal reflux disease and recurrent urinary tract infections.
Her asthma was treated with a combination preparation containing both salmeterol (25 microg) and fluticasone (500 microg) of which she was taking two puffs, twice per day. Thus a total dose of 2,000 microg per day of fluticasone was given for 3 months prior to her presentation. She always rinsed and gargled post inhaler, but did not use a spacer. It had been more than 7 months since her last course of oral prednisolone. She also used salbutamol nebules as required. Her only non-asthma medication was omeprazole at a dose of 20 mg twice daily.
She did not have any other systemic or localizing symptoms and had no other immunosuppressive medications or conditions. She was a non-smoker and had no known cryptococcal exposure.
At microlaryngoscopy her right true cord was found to be inflamed, with focal erythroleukoplakia (see Figure 3). Bronchoscopy and oesophagoscopy were normal. Histopathological examination of the biopsies of the involved fold revealed focal ulceration, underlying granulation tissue, and heavy lymphocyte and plasma cell infiltration. Aggregates of Cryptococcus organisms, as confirmed by periodic acid-Schiff and methanamine silver staining, lay in the surface inflammatory crust and within the subepithelial stroma (see Figures 4 and 5). There was no hyperplasia, cellular atypia, or signs of malignancy. Her cryptococcal serum antigen recorded a very low positive of 2 via the latex agglutination test. Her fasting glucose was unremarkable at 5 mmol/l. Her CXR was within normal limits, and her HIV test was negative.
Treatment involved oral antifungals and a reduction in her inhaled corticosteroid. She was instructed to reduce her inhaled fluticasone back to a daily maximum dose of 1,000 microg per day, and was placed on fluconazole at 200 mg twice a day.
She noticed improvement in her voice within weeks and after 5 months of fluconazole treatment her voice had returned to baseline. Stroboscopy 4 months into treatment revealed a near normal right true vocal fold with only slightly prominent vasculature, and near normal mucosal wave.
Her fluconazole was ceased after 8 months of treatment. Her voice remains normal off fluconazole, and at the lower dose of fluticasone.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 69-year-old female on high-dose inhaled fluticasone for asthma presented with a 1-month history of hoarseness and post-nasal drip.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed progressive hoarseness and post-nasal drip 1 month prior to presentation, 3 months after increasing her inhaled fluticasone dose to 2,000 ug/day (taken without a spacer) for moderate persistent asthma.
subjective.past_medical_history: 10-year history of moderate persistent asthma (requiring 1-2 short courses of oral prednisolone per year, last course >7 months prior), gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), and recurrent urinary tract infections; non-smoker with no known cryptococcal exposure.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for hoarseness and post-nasal drip. Negative for systemic symptoms. Home medications: inhaled salmeterol/fluticasone (25/500 ug, 2 puffs twice daily; total fluticasone 2,000 ug/day), PRN salbutamol nebules, and oral omeprazole 20 mg twice daily.

objective.physical_examination: Microlaryngoscopy revealed an inflamed right true vocal cord with focal erythroleukoplakia.
objective.routine_investigations: Serum cryptococcal antigen latex agglutination test was weakly positive at a titer of 1:2; fasting blood glucose was normal (5 mmol/L), HIV test was negative, and chest radiograph was normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Bronchoscopy and esophagoscopy were normal. Right true vocal fold biopsy histopathology showed focal ulceration, granulation tissue, heavy lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltration, and aggregates of Cryptococcus organisms in the surface inflammatory crust and subepithelial stroma confirmed by periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) and methenamine silver staining, without dysplasia or malignancy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis of isolated right true vocal cord laryngeal cryptococcosis associated with high-dose inhaled fluticasone therapy, confirmed by vocal fold biopsy PAS and methenamine silver histopathology and low-positive serum CrAg latex agglutination (titer 1:2). Treated with oral fluconazole 200 mg twice daily for 8 months alongside reduction of inhaled fluticasone to a maximum of 1,000 ug/day, achieving near-normal vocal fold stroboscopy at 4 months, full return to baseline voice by 5 months, and sustained remission off fluconazole.
